## The problem

Voice Commander operates a Mac for someone who can't use their hands. You say "computer,
open YouTube", "click the third one", "turn it up", "commit my changes", and it does it:
opening sites, driving the browser, typing, clicking, adjusting volume, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth,
and running terminal commands. Simple questions ("what's 70 Fahrenheit in Celsius?") it
answers directly, without touching any tools.

Every model runs on the laptop:

- **Speech to text:** Whisper large-v3-turbo (`mlx-community/whisper-large-v3-turbo`,
  about 1.6 GB) on the GPU through MLX, with Hugging Face forced offline. Downloading it is
  the only step that ever goes online.
- **The agent:** Qwen 3.8 27B (`qwen3.8:27b-mlx`, about 18 GB) served by Ollama on
  `127.0.0.1`, using its native tool calling. Any local model that supports tool calling
  can be swapped in with `--model`, but the client refuses any server that isn't on the
  loopback address.
- **Speech out:** macOS `say`, with three presets you can switch between by voice
  ("computer, use the british voice"): a flat monotone by default, British and American. The
  choice is remembered across restarts. Replies go in on stdin, never as an argument, so a
  reply like "-o /tmp/x" can't turn into a `say` option.

So commands and audio never leave the machine.

A voice agent with control of a computer has an unusual threat model:

- **Anyone or anything can speak.** A TV, a video the agent itself opened, a visitor.
- **The model reads untrusted text.** Web pages, tab titles and terminal output can contain
  instructions aimed at it.
- **It holds remote-control rights.** macOS Accessibility and Automation permissions are,
  in effect, permission to do anything a user could.

So the design starts from one rule: **neither the model nor the microphone gets the final
word on anything risky.**

## Who is it talking to?

Every utterance passes through a gate before the model sees it. A wake word has to *start*
the utterance, so "I bought a new computer" on TV doesn't count. After the assistant
replies, a short window accepts an answer without the wake word, so a plain "yes" can
confirm something. Stop phrases work at any time. Everything else is dropped without being
logged, and no audio is ever written to disk.

Try it. This is a small JavaScript port of the real gate:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
examples = [
  "computer, open YouTube",
  "I bought a new computer last week",
  "hey jarvis, turn the volume down",
  "yes",
  "computer",
  "computer thank you for watching",
  "OK stop everything right now"
]
viewof example = Inputs.select(examples, {label: "Example"})
viewof utterance = Inputs.text({label: "Or type one", value: example, width: 360})
viewof followUp = Inputs.toggle({label: "Just replied", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wakeWords = ["computer", "jarvis"]
stopPhrases = ["stop everything", "emergency stop", "kill switch", "abort program", "halt program"]
// Whisper's well-known inventions on silence or noise.
hallucinations = new Set(["", "you", "thank you", "thanks", "thank you very much",
  "thanks for watching", "thank you for watching", "bye", "bye bye", "please subscribe",
  "subscribe", "like and subscribe", "so", "okay", "hmm", "um", "uh"])
normalise = t => t.toLowerCase().replace(/[^\p{L}\p{N}_\s']/gu, " ").split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).join(" ")
wake = new RegExp(String.raw`^\W*(?:(?:hey|hi|ok|okay)\W+)?(?:${wakeWords.join("|")})\b\W*`, "i")

function decide(text, followUpOpen) {
  const norm = normalise(text)
  const stop = stopPhrases.find(p => norm.includes(p))
  if (stop) return {kind: "stop", why: `Contains the stop phrase "${stop}". Halts at once, addressed or not; a false stop is harmless.`}
  const m = text.match(wake)
  if (m) {
    const rest = text.slice(m[0].length).trim()
    if (hallucinations.has(normalise(rest)))
      return {kind: "wake", why: "Wake word on its own (or followed by a typical Whisper hallucination). Chimes and waits for the command."}
    return {kind: "command", text: rest, why: "Starts with a wake word. The rest goes to the model."}
  }
  if (followUpOpen && !hallucinations.has(norm))
    return {kind: "command", text: text.trim(), why: "No wake word, but the follow-up window is open, so it's treated as a reply."}
  const midSentence = wakeWords.some(w => norm.split(" ").includes(w))
  return {kind: "ignore", why: midSentence
    ? "A wake word appears, but not at the start. Dropped and not logged."
    : "Not addressed to the assistant. Dropped and not logged."}
}

decision = decide(utterance, followUp)
html`<div class="gate-result gate-${decision.kind}">
  <strong>${decision.kind.toUpperCase()}</strong>${decision.text ? html` → <code>${decision.text}</code>` : ""}
  <div>${decision.why}</div>
</div>`
```

## The voice loop

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  A["Microphone<br/>(echo-cancelled)"] --> B["Energy-based detector<br/>cuts audio into utterances"]
  B --> C["Whisper on MLX<br/>(offline)"]
  C --> D{"Its own<br/>voice?"}
  D -- yes --> X["Drop"]
  D -- no --> G{"Gate"}
  G -- "stop phrase" --> K["Halt mid-turn"]
  G -- ignore --> X
  G -- command --> M["Local model<br/>(tool calling)"]
  M --> P{"Policy<br/>checks"}
  P -- refused --> R["Say why"]
  P -- "needs a yes" --> Y["Read the action back,<br/>wait for an exact yes"]
  P -- allowed --> T["Run the tool<br/>(fixed argv, no shell)"]
  Y --> T
  T --> S["Speak or show a short reply,<br/>open 8 s follow-up"]
```

You can interrupt it while it talks. The microphone and the assistant's voice share one
`AVAudioEngine` with macOS voice processing on (the same echo canceller FaceTime uses). As
a backstop, any transcript that matches what it's saying, or said in the last 2 seconds, is
dropped, so its own voice can never become a command even if cancellation is imperfect. If
voice processing can't start, it falls back to ignoring the microphone while it speaks.

When you don't want it talking, "computer, voice off" (or muting the Mac) switches replies
to a small panel in the corner of the screen that fades after a few seconds, and "dismiss"
hides it. Confirmation questions are the exception: they're always spoken, and stay on
screen for the full 30 seconds you have to answer, so you always know what you're saying
yes to.

## Treating the model as untrusted

The model can only call the tools in one file, and every call is checked against its schema
before anything runs. On top of that:

**Tool results are data, not instructions.** Text from web pages, apps, files and the
terminal comes back wrapped in a tag the model is told never to take orders from, and the
wrapper can't be closed from inside:

```python
def _untrusted(name: str, result: str) -> str:
    body = result.replace("<", "‹").replace(">", "›")
    return f'<untrusted_tool_result tool="{name}">\n{body}\n</untrusted_tool_result>'
```

After two refusals the turn ends, so the model can't keep hunting for a workaround. After
three minutes without a command the conversation is cleared, so old page text doesn't
linger into a new request.

**Confirmation is decided in code.** `git push`, `uv add`, clicking Send, Post, Buy or Pay,
pressing Return in a messaging app and typing into password fields all need a spoken yes.
The agent reads the action back, and the code, not the model, checks the next utterance:

```python
pending = self._take_pending()          # expires after 30 seconds
if pending is not None:
    if norm in YES:
        return self._run_confirmed(pending)
    self._log_tool(pending.name, pending.args, "cancelled")
```

The `confirmed` flag that unlocks the action isn't in any tool schema, so the model has no
way to set it. Deleting is refused outright, and a yes never unlocks a refused action.

**An allowlist for the terminal, because a denylist for a shell is a losing game.**
Commands run as fixed argument lists, never through a shell, with a 20-second timeout.
There's no `rm`, `mv`, `cp` or `sudo`, and no pipes, redirects, chaining or substitution.
Git is limited to everyday subcommands, without forcing or deleting flags:

```python
for arg in args[1:]:
    flag = arg.split("=", 1)[0]
    if flag in GIT_BANNED_FLAGS:
        raise ActionRefused(f"git {flag} can lose work, so it isn't allowed by voice")
    if re.fullmatch(r"-[A-Za-z]{2,}", arg) and GIT_BANNED_SHORT & set(arg[1:]):
        raise ActionRefused(f"git {arg} includes a forcing or deleting flag")
```

Clicks are refused when the target's label sounds destructive (Delete, Bin, Erase, Don't
Save, Forget), and refused outright if the target can't be inspected. Disk Utility,
Keychain Access, Script Editor, Automator and Shortcuts can't be opened by voice.

Every command heard and every tool call (allowed, refused, confirmed or cancelled) is logged
to a file only the user can read. "Stop everything" is matched before the model sees it,
and a global hotkey (⌃⌥⌘S) stops it from anywhere.

## Keeping permissions narrow

Whatever app holds Accessibility and Automation, everything running inside it inherits
them: every script, package install and coding agent in that terminal. So the permissions
belong to a small Swift menu-bar app that launches the agent, not to Terminal, and the
README walks through removing them from Terminal afterwards.

The agent also avoids needing them at all where it can:

| Task | Route that needs no Accessibility |
|---|---|
| Open a site, video or playlist | `open "https://…"` |
| Volume | `osascript -e "set volume output volume 70"` |
| Browser navigation | Brave's AppleScript dictionary |
| Wi-Fi / Bluetooth | `networksetup`, `blueutil` |

Simulated typing and clicking are the fallback: they're what a hands-free user ultimately
needs, but they're the reason the app needs Accessibility in the first place.

A `--dry-run` mode checks and shows every tool call without running it, and needs no
permissions at all.

## How it was built

Test-driven throughout, red-green-refactor: 473 tests that run in under a second, in 57
small commits. The policy layer is kept free of side effects so it's easy to test
exhaustively, and the clock and model server are injected so timing and model replies can be faked. Python with uv,
MLX Whisper for speech, Ollama for the model, AVFoundation through PyObjC for audio, and a
Swift launcher for the menu-bar app.

## Known gaps

The safety rules are best-effort, and the README says so:

- **Anyone can still speak.** A video the agent opened could say "computer, …" at the start
  of a sentence, and anyone can answer inside the 8-second follow-up window. Echo
  cancellation only removes the assistant's own voice. Speaker verification is the next step.
- Keyboard shortcuts inside apps that delete (such as `#` in Gmail), Return on a focused
  Delete button, and terminals inside editors such as VS Code aren't caught.
- It needs an Apple Silicon Mac with about 32 GB of memory for the default model.
